title: Patient Care Fundamentals
summary: The hands-on basic care that fills most of a tech's shift: hygiene, toileting, skin, feeding, mobility, transfers, fall prevention, comfort and the end of life. The work that patients remember and that surveys and lawsuits are built on.

lessons.title: Dignity, privacy, and the conversation that starts every task
lessons.body:
Almost everything a technician does to a patient is something an adult normally does alone and behind a closed door. Washing, undressing, urinating, being turned over. The body does not stop needing those things because it is sick, but the person's control over them disappears the moment they are in a gown on a stretcher. That loss of control, more than pain, is what patients describe afterward as the worst part.

So the skill is not the washcloth. The skill is giving back as much control as the situation allows, in the seconds before you start.

### The four moves, every time

1. **Knock and wait**, even on a curtain. Say your name and your role. "I'm Jose, I'm the tech taking care of you."
2. **Say what you are about to do and why**, in one sentence with no jargon. "The nurse needs a urine sample, so I'm going to help you to the bathroom."
3. **Ask permission and offer a choice.** "Is now okay, or do you want a few minutes?" A real choice, even a small one, is the whole point.
4. **Close the curtain and the door, and cover what you are not working on.** Expose one area at a time.

A patient who says no is exercising a right. You do not argue and you do not do it anyway. You say "okay," find out what the objection is, and tell the nurse. A refusal is clinical information, not an obstacle.

### Language that keeps people adult

Say `brief` or `underwear`, not "diaper." Say `bedpan`, not "potty." Do not call an adult "sweetie," "honey," or "buddy" — use the name they give you, and use their last name with a title until they tell you otherwise. Never talk over a patient to a coworker about that patient.

Assume every patient hears you, including the intubated, the intoxicated, the demented and the arresting. Hearing is the last sense to go and families are listening from the doorway.

> **Key:** Announce, explain, ask, cover. Four moves, about eight seconds, and they convert an invasion into care.

### Chaperones and boundaries

Any exam or care involving genitals, breasts or rectum gets a chaperone, and the chaperone's name goes in the chart. This protects the patient and it protects you. If a patient becomes sexually inappropriate, you stop, state the boundary once in a flat voice — "That is not okay, I'm going to step out" — leave, and tell the charge nurse. You do not laugh it off.

> **On shift:** The patient satisfaction question hospitals actually get scored on is whether staff treated them with courtesy and respect. The tech is in the room more than anyone. That score is largely yours.
keyPoints: Knock, introduce, explain in one plain sentence, ask permission, then cover everything you are not working on.
A refusal is a right and a piece of clinical information — report it, never override it.
Chaperone any care involving genitals, breasts or rectum, and document the chaperone's name.
Use adult words: brief not diaper, bedpan not potty, their name not 'sweetie'.
Assume every patient hears you, including the sedated, demented and intubated.

checks.q: A patient tells you she does not want a bath right now. What do you do?
choices: Explain that it is hospital policy and proceed gently
Accept the refusal, ask what her concern is, and tell the nurse
Wait ten minutes and start without asking again
Ask a family member to convince her
checks.why: A competent patient may refuse any care. Your job is to accept it, learn why (pain? nausea? modesty?), and pass it on. Proceeding after a refusal is battery, and 'policy' is not consent.

checks.q: Which piece of care requires a chaperone whose name is documented?
choices: Applying an ECG electrode to the ankle
Assisting with a pelvic exam
Handing a patient a warm blanket
Taking a blood pressure on the upper arm
checks.why: Care involving genitals, breasts or rectum gets a chaperone and the chaperone is charted. The other three involve no intimate exposure.

checks.q: Which phrase belongs in an adult ED room?
choices: "Let's get that diaper changed, sweetie."
"Mr. Ruiz, I need to change your brief. Is now okay?"
"She's a total care, can you grab me a diaper?" (said over the patient)
"Hold still, honey, this won't take a second."
checks.why: Name plus title, the adult word 'brief', a plain statement of the task, and a request for permission. The others infantilize the patient or talk about her in front of her.

lessons.title: Bathing, oral care, and the skin you see while you wash
lessons.body:
A bed bath in the emergency department is rarely about cleanliness for its own sake. It happens because a patient arrived soiled, because blood or vomit has to come off before imaging, because a nursing home patient is being admitted, or because the skin has to be seen. The wash is also the most complete skin assessment anyone will do on that patient all day, so you look while you work.

### The sequence, and why it runs this way

Water at about `105 to 110 F` (`41 to 43 C`) — warm on the inside of your wrist, never hot. Two basins or a pack of disposable cloths, gloves, and towels ready before you start, because you do not leave an exposed patient to go find soap.

Work **clean to dirty, top to bottom**: eyes first (inner corner outward, a fresh corner of the cloth per eye), then face, neck, arms, chest and abdomen, legs, back, and perineum last. The reason is simple transfer of organisms — the perineum and the skin folds carry the heaviest bacterial load, so they never touch anything that goes back on the face.

Expose one body part at a time and dry it before you move on. Wet skin between fingers, toes, under breasts, in the groin and under an abdominal fold (`pannus`) macerates and breaks down within a day.

### Perineal care

Female: separate the labia, wipe **front to back**, one downward stroke per surface, new cloth surface each stroke. Back to front drags bowel flora into the urethra and is a direct route to a urinary tract infection.

Male: clean the tip in a circular motion moving outward from the meatus. If the patient is uncircumcised, retract the foreskin, clean, and **replace it**. A foreskin left retracted swells and can strangle the glans (`paraphimosis`) — a real emergency caused by a forgotten step.

If a urinary catheter is in, clean the first few inches of tubing moving *away* from the body, never toward it.

> **Trap:** Front to back is the single most tested detail in perineal care, and the retracted foreskin is the most common real-world harm.

### Oral care

Teeth, gums and tongue get brushed twice a shift for anyone who cannot do it themselves. For an unconscious patient: head of bed up if allowed, head **turned to the side**, suction within reach, a barely moist swab or toothbrush, and no free water in the mouth. Dentures come out, get labeled with the patient's name, and go in a denture cup — not wrapped in a napkin on the tray, which is how they end up in the trash and on an incident report.

> **On shift:** While you wash, call out what you find — a heel that is red and does not blanch, a rash under the breast, a wound nobody has charted. Say it to the nurse and chart it. The bath is the exam.
keyPoints: Bath water is 105 to 110 F; test it on your wrist, never on a scalded or neuropathic patient's word alone.
Clean to dirty, top to bottom, perineum last; expose and dry one part at a time.
Female peri care is front to back, one stroke per cloth surface; male uncircumcised care ends by replacing the foreskin.
Unconscious oral care: head of bed up, head turned, suction ready, no free water.
Dentures go in a labeled cup, never in a napkin.

checks.q: You retract the foreskin of an uncircumcised patient to clean the glans. What must happen before you finish?
choices: Apply a barrier cream to the retracted skin
Leave it retracted so the area stays dry
Return the foreskin to its normal position
Tape the foreskin back for the nurse to inspect
checks.why: A foreskin left retracted causes swelling and paraphimosis, which can cut off blood flow to the glans. Replacing it is a required step, not an option.

checks.q: Why is the perineum washed last in a bed bath?
choices: Because it is the most painful area
Because it carries the heaviest bacterial load and must not contaminate cleaner skin
Because water cools by then and cool water is preferred there
Because the nurse must witness it
checks.why: Clean to dirty prevents transferring perineal and fold flora to the face and trunk. Water temperature and pain are not the reason, and no witness is required for routine peri care.

checks.q: You are doing oral care on an unresponsive patient. Which setup is correct?
choices: Flat in bed, rinse with a cup of water, suction afterward
Head of bed elevated, head turned to the side, suction at the bedside, minimal moisture
Head of bed elevated, patient supine and face up, irrigate generously
Flat with head turned, no suction needed for swabs
checks.why: Elevation plus a turned head lets secretions drain out rather than down the airway, and suction must be immediately available. Free water in the mouth of someone who cannot protect their airway causes aspiration.

lessons.title: Toileting: bedpans, urinals, commodes and incontinence
lessons.body:
Patients hold it. They hold it because calling for a bedpan is humiliating, because nobody answered last time, and because they do not want to be a bother. Held urine causes agitation in the elderly, a falsely high heart rate, and eventually a fall when they try to get up alone at 0300. Offering toileting on a schedule — roughly every two hours while awake — prevents more falls than any alarm.

### Choosing the equipment

| Device | Use it when |
|---|---|
| Bathroom | Patient can walk and is not on strict bed rest or continuous monitoring |
| Bedside commode | Can stand and pivot but cannot walk safely down the hall |
| Urinal | Male, can sit or stand, needs to void only |
| Standard bedpan | Can lift the hips or be rolled |
| Fracture pan | Hip fracture, spinal precautions, post-op hip, or anyone who cannot lift — the shallow end goes under the buttocks |

The fracture pan is the one people get backward. Its thin, tapered edge slides under a patient who cannot raise their pelvis; the **shallow end faces the head of the bed** and the deep, open end faces the feet.

### The technique

Warm the pan under running water and dry it — cold metal or plastic against skin makes people clench. Powder or a barrier wipe on the rim reduces sticking. Raise the head of the bed to about `30 to 45 degrees` if the patient's condition allows, because nobody can defecate flat on their back; the position closes the angle the rectum needs.

If the patient can lift: knees bent, feet flat, "push through your heels and lift on three." If not: roll them toward you onto their side, place the pan against the buttocks, and roll them back onto it.

Then leave. Put the call bell in their hand, toilet paper and wipes within reach, curtain closed, and step out. Come back in `no more than 5 minutes` and check. Sitting on a bedpan is a documented cause of pressure injury on the sacrum — `15 minutes` is too long.

> **Key:** Never leave a patient on a bedpan longer than about five minutes without checking, and never leave a confused patient on one alone at all.

### Incontinence and the skin

Stool and urine on skin cause `incontinence-associated dermatitis` — a red, weeping, burning breakdown that is not a pressure injury and does not respond to repositioning. Clean it off promptly with a pH-balanced cleanser, pat dry, and apply a barrier cream with `zinc oxide` or dimethicone. Do not scrub.

A brief is a last resort, not a default. Putting a continent person in one teaches learned incontinence in a single admission. If a patient in a brief is continent, say so to the nurse.

> **On shift:** Measure and report output before you dump it. Volume, color, clarity, odor, and whether there was blood. "About 400 mL, dark amber, cloudy" is charting. "Voided" is not.
keyPoints: Offer toileting about every 2 hours while awake — scheduled toileting prevents falls better than alarms.
Fracture pan for hip fracture, spinal precautions or anyone who cannot lift the pelvis; shallow end toward the head.
Head of bed 30 to 45 degrees for a bedpan; nobody defecates flat on their back.
Check back within 5 minutes — a bedpan is a pressure injury device after that.
Incontinence dermatitis is treated by prompt cleansing and a zinc oxide or dimethicone barrier, not by turning.

checks.q: An 81-year-old with a suspected hip fracture needs to move her bowels. Which device and orientation?
choices: Standard bedpan, deep end toward the head
Fracture pan, shallow tapered end under the buttocks toward the head of the bed
Bedside commode with a two-person pivot transfer
Standard bedpan after log-rolling onto the fractured side
checks.why: A fracture pan is designed to slide under a pelvis that cannot lift, with the thin end toward the head. A standard pan requires hip elevation, and transferring or rolling onto a fractured hip causes harm.

checks.q: You place a patient on a bedpan and step out. When should you return?
choices: Within 5 minutes, and sooner if she is confused
When she presses the call bell, however long that takes
After 15 to 20 minutes so she is not rushed
At the end of your rounding hour
checks.why: Prolonged bedpan sitting concentrates pressure on the sacrum and causes skin injury. Five minutes is the working limit, and a confused patient should not be left alone on one at all.

checks.q: A patient's perineum is bright red, weeping and painful after hours of diarrhea. What is this and what does it need?
choices: A stage 2 pressure injury; turn every 2 hours
Incontinence-associated dermatitis; prompt cleansing and a zinc oxide or dimethicone barrier
Cellulitis; the area should be left open to air only
A fungal rash; apply the patient's home steroid cream
checks.why: Moisture and stool enzymes cause a chemical dermatitis distinct from pressure injury. It resolves with prompt cleansing and a barrier product; repositioning alone does not fix it, and treating it as infection delays care.

lessons.title: Making the bed, and the linen nobody thinks about
lessons.body:
A stretcher is remade dozens of times a shift and it is one of the few tasks you will genuinely be judged on for speed. It is also an infection control task and a skin protection task, which is why there is a right way.

### Unoccupied: the two rules

Work **one entire side, then the other**. Bottom sheet, draw sheet or slide sheet, top linen, then walk around once. Going back and forth doubles the steps and is the single reason people are slow at this.

Keep the bottom layer **wrinkle-free and taut**. A fold in a draw sheet under a sacrum concentrates pressure into a line, and in an eight-hour ED boarding stay that line becomes a pressure injury. Smooth is not cosmetic.

A **draw sheet or slide sheet** goes on every bed, positioned from the patient's shoulders to mid-thigh. It is what you will use to boost, turn and lateral-transfer them, and it has to be under the torso to work.

### Occupied: roll, do half, roll back

For a patient who cannot get out of bed: flatten the bed if tolerated, lower the rail on your side, and roll the patient away from you onto their side with the far rail up. Loosen and fan-fold the soiled linen lengthwise against their back. Place the clean bottom sheet and draw sheet on the empty half, fan-folding the excess tight against the dirty bundle. Raise your rail, go to the other side, roll the patient over both ridges, remove the dirty linen into the bag, and pull the clean through.

Two people is the standard, one on each side, for anyone heavy, confused, or attached to lines. One person plus a rolling patient is how a tube gets pulled out.

### Linen handling

- **Hold soiled linen away from your body and your uniform.** Never against the chest, which is the classic competency failure.
- **Never shake linen.** Shaking aerosolizes skin cells, spores and `Clostridioides difficile`.
- **Never put linen on the floor.** Floor to bed and bed to floor are both contamination events.
- Roll the dirty bundle **inward**, soiled side inside, and bag it at the point of use.
- Linen that leaks goes in a designated impervious bag; what counts as isolation linen varies by facility policy.
- **Clean linen that enters a patient room does not leave it.** If you carry in an extra blanket and do not use it, it is discarded, not returned to the shelf.

> **Trap:** Grabbing a stack of linen "just in case" and then walking it out to the next room. Every item that crossed the threshold is now contaminated.

> **On shift:** Two blankets in the warmer and a fresh flat sheet under a patient who has been on a hard stretcher for six hours is the cheapest comfort intervention in the department, and the one families thank you for.
keyPoints: Complete one whole side of the bed before moving to the other — it halves the walking and the time.
The bottom layer must be taut; a wrinkle under the sacrum becomes a pressure injury during a long boarding stay.
A draw or slide sheet from shoulders to mid-thigh goes on every bed, because it is your boosting and turning tool.
Never shake linen, never put it on the floor, and hold soiled linen away from your uniform.
Clean linen that enters a room stays in that room.

checks.q: Why is shaking out a sheet forbidden?
choices: It wrinkles the fabric and increases pressure injury risk
It aerosolizes skin cells and organisms such as C. difficile spores
It violates fire code in an oxygen-enriched room
It shortens the life of hospital linen
checks.why: Shaking launches contaminated particles into the room air and onto surfaces. Wrinkles matter, but that is a separate reason and is fixed by smoothing, not by refraining from shaking.

checks.q: You bring three warm blankets into an isolation room and use one. What happens to the other two?
choices: Return them to the blanket warmer
Place them on the clean linen cart outside the room
Discard or launder them; they do not leave the room for reuse
Fold them into the patient's belongings bag
checks.why: Anything that crosses into the patient zone is considered contaminated. Returning it to a warmer or a clean cart spreads organisms to every future patient.

checks.q: Where should the draw sheet sit on the bed?
choices: From the head of the bed to the knees
From the shoulders to mid-thigh
Under the hips only, about 18 inches wide
Under the heels and calves
checks.why: Shoulders to mid-thigh captures the torso and pelvis, the mass you actually lift. A sheet under the hips alone tears or slides, and one at the heels does nothing for turning.

lessons.title: Skin: pressure injury, the turn schedule, and what a stage means
lessons.body:
Pressure injury is a mechanical problem. Skin and the tissue under it are squeezed between a bone and a surface; the capillaries collapse; oxygen stops arriving. Muscle dies before skin does, because muscle needs more oxygen — which is why the visible spot is the small end of a much bigger cone of dead tissue underneath.

The damage starts in **1 to 2 hours** of unrelieved pressure. That matters in an emergency department, because a patient who lay on a hard backboard, then a hard stretcher, then boarded for nine hours has been under continuous pressure the whole time and nobody counted it.

### Where they form

Supine: **sacrum and heels** first, then occiput, scapulae and elbows. Side-lying: greater trochanter, the ear, the lateral malleolus. Sitting: ischial tuberosities. Add the device injuries a tech creates — under an oxygen tubing loop over the ear, under a pulse oximeter probe left on the same finger, under a cervical collar, under a nasal cannula at the nares.

### The stages, in plain words

| Stage | What you see |
|---|---|
| 1 | Intact skin, redness that does **not blanch** when you press it |
| 2 | Partial thickness loss: shallow open ulcer or an intact or ruptured blister; pink, moist, no slough |
| 3 | Full thickness: fat visible, may have slough, no bone/tendon/muscle showing |
| 4 | Full thickness with **bone, tendon or muscle** exposed |
| Unstageable | Base covered by slough or eschar so depth cannot be judged |
| Deep tissue injury | Intact or blistered skin that is **deep purple or maroon** — injury from below |

The blanch test is the whole of stage 1. Press the red area with a fingertip for about `3 seconds` and release. If it turns white and then pinks back up, blood flow is intact — that is transient redness. If it stays red, capillaries are already damaged.

> **Key:** Non-blanchable redness is a stage 1 pressure injury and must be reported and charted the moment you see it, which is usually during a bath or a turn.

### Prevention, which is your job

- **Reposition at least every 2 hours** in bed, every `1 hour` in a chair — or teach a shift of weight every `15 minutes` if they can do it themselves.
- **Float the heels.** A pillow lengthwise under the calves so the heels touch nothing. Do not put a pillow *under* the heels; that just moves the pressure.
- Use the **30-degree lateral tilt**, not a full 90-degree side-lying position, which loads the trochanter directly.
- Keep skin clean and dry; barrier cream where there is moisture.
- **Do not massage a reddened bony prominence.** It shears already-damaged capillaries.
- **Do not use a ring or donut cushion.** It creates a circle of ischemia around the area it is meant to protect.
- Lift or slide with a sheet — never drag. Dragging produces `shear`, which tears the tissue planes under intact skin.

> **On shift:** On arrival, look under the collar, under the heels and at the sacrum, and say what you find out loud. An injury present on arrival that gets documented in the ED belongs to the nursing home. One that gets found on the floor at hour twelve belongs to your hospital.
keyPoints: Unrelieved pressure damages tissue in 1 to 2 hours; muscle dies before the skin shows it.
Stage 1 is non-blanchable redness on intact skin — press 3 seconds and watch.
Reposition at least every 2 hours in bed and every hour in a chair; 30-degree tilt, not 90.
Float heels on a pillow under the calves; never massage a red bony prominence; never use a donut cushion.
Deep tissue injury looks purple or maroon under intact skin and means damage from below.

checks.q: You press a red area over a patient's sacrum for 3 seconds. It stays red. What is this?
choices: Normal reactive hyperemia, no action needed
A stage 1 pressure injury that must be reported and documented
A stage 2 pressure injury
Incontinence-associated dermatitis
checks.why: Non-blanchable erythema on intact skin defines stage 1. Blanchable redness would be reactive hyperemia. Stage 2 requires skin loss or a blister, and dermatitis is a moisture injury with a different pattern.

checks.q: How should heels be protected in a supine patient?
choices: A donut cushion around each heel
A pillow placed directly under the heels
A pillow lengthwise under the calves so the heels hang free
Massage the heels every two hours to restore circulation
checks.why: Floating the heels removes pressure entirely. A pillow under the heels just relocates it, a donut creates a ring of ischemia, and massaging damaged tissue worsens it.

checks.q: A wound over the sacrum shows exposed tendon. How is it staged?
choices: Stage 2
Stage 3
Stage 4
Unstageable
checks.why: Visible bone, tendon or muscle defines stage 4. Stage 3 exposes fat but not those structures, and unstageable means slough or eschar hides the base so depth cannot be judged.

lessons.title: Feeding, swallowing, and aspiration precautions
lessons.body:
Swallowing is a reflex that briefly shuts the airway. The epiglottis drops, the vocal cords close, breathing pauses, and the bolus goes past. If the timing is off by a fraction of a second — after a stroke, with dementia, with sedation, with a tracheostomy, in a frail 90-year-old — food goes into the trachea instead. That is `aspiration`, and aspiration pneumonia kills a substantial share of the elderly patients who get it.

### Nothing by mouth until somebody clears it

In an emergency department the default for a new stroke, a new altered mental status, anyone waiting on a procedure, and anyone who sounds wet is `NPO` — nothing by mouth, including water and ice chips. An ice chip is water. Every stroke patient gets a **bedside swallow screen** before the first sip, and that screen is a nurse or speech-language pathology function, not a tech function. If a family member is feeding a patient who has not been cleared, you stop it politely and tell the nurse.

Before you hand anyone a tray, check the board and the chart for the diet order and for `NPO`. Techs handing a sandwich to an NPO patient is one of the most common safety events in an ED.

### How to feed safely

- **Sit them up to `90 degrees`.** Fully upright, hips flexed, not reclined. If they cannot leave the bed, head of bed all the way up.
- **Chin tucked slightly down** toward the chest while swallowing. Tucking narrows the airway entrance and widens the food path. Never tip the head back — that opens the airway.
- Small bites, half a teaspoon. **One bite at a time, and check the mouth is empty before the next.**
- Alternate solids and liquids only if allowed; some patients are on thickened liquids (`nectar`, `honey` or `pudding` consistency) precisely because thin liquids run ahead of the reflex.
- **No straws** for an aspiration-risk patient — a straw delivers a fast bolus to the back of the throat.
- Sit at eye level. Do not stand over them, and do not rush. A hurried feed is an unsafe feed.
- **Keep them upright for `30 to 60 minutes` after eating.**
- Oral care after every meal; pooled food plus mouth bacteria is what actually seeds aspiration pneumonia.

### The signs you stop for

Coughing or throat-clearing during or right after swallowing. A **wet or gurgly voice** after a sip — have them say their name after swallowing and listen. Drooling, pocketing food in a cheek, food falling from the mouth, watering eyes, a change in breathing, or `SpO2` dropping a few points during the meal. Stop, sit them upright, suction if trained and equipped, and get the nurse.

> **Trap:** Silent aspiration. Up to half of stroke patients who aspirate never cough. No cough does not mean it went down the right way — that is why the screen exists.

> **On shift:** Record how much they actually ate as a fraction or percentage, and the fluid volume in milliliters. `"Ate 50% of tray, 240 mL apple juice"` is intake documentation. "Tolerated diet" is not.
keyPoints: NPO means nothing by mouth including ice chips; a stroke patient needs a bedside swallow screen before the first sip.
Feed at 90 degrees upright with the chin tucked down, never with the head tipped back.
Half-teaspoon bites, mouth empty before the next, no straws for aspiration risk, upright 30 to 60 minutes after.
Wet or gurgly voice, coughing, pocketing and a falling SpO2 during a meal mean stop and call the nurse.
Silent aspiration is common after stroke — the absence of a cough proves nothing.

checks.q: Which head position is correct for a patient at risk of aspiration?
choices: Head extended back to straighten the throat
Head neutral with the chin tucked slightly toward the chest
Head turned fully to the weak side with the neck extended
Reclined at 30 degrees with the chin raised
checks.why: A chin tuck narrows the laryngeal opening and protects the airway. Extending the neck opens the airway directly to the bolus, and reclining lets food travel by gravity before the reflex fires.

checks.q: A stroke patient's daughter is giving her ice chips in the hallway. The patient has not had a swallow screen. What do you do?
choices: Nothing; ice chips are not food
Allow it but document the amount
Politely stop it, explain that a swallow check is needed first, and tell the nurse
Substitute thickened liquid from the pantry
checks.why: Ice is water and thin water is the highest-risk consistency. NPO stands until a bedside swallow screen is passed, and choosing a thickened substitute yourself is making a diet decision you cannot make.

checks.q: Halfway through a meal, a patient's voice sounds wet and gurgly and her SpO2 drops from 96% to 92%. What is your first action?
choices: Offer water to clear her throat
Stop the meal, keep her fully upright, and get the nurse
Lay her flat and turn her head to the side
Finish the meal quickly so she can rest
checks.why: A wet voice with a falling saturation is aspiration until proven otherwise. Stopping and sitting upright protects the airway. Water adds volume, and laying her flat removes the only protection gravity is giving.

lessons.title: Output: urine, stool, emesis, drains and the ostomy
lessons.body:
Output is data. In an emergency department it is often the fastest read on whether a patient is perfusing, bleeding or obstructed, and the tech is usually the only person who actually sees it. Nothing gets dumped before it is measured and described.

### Urine

Normal adult output is about `0.5 mL/kg/hour` — roughly `30 to 50 mL/hour`, or `1 to 2 L` a day. Below `30 mL/hour` in an adult is `oliguria` and gets reported now; it is an early sign of shock, dehydration or obstruction. Zero output can mean a blocked or kinked catheter rather than a failing kidney, so look at the tubing before you announce renal failure.

Describe color and clarity: pale yellow is well hydrated, dark amber is concentrated, cloudy with odor suggests infection, red or tea-colored suggests blood or muscle breakdown (`rhabdomyolysis`), and orange can simply be `phenazopyridine`, a bladder analgesic.

Keep the drainage bag **below the level of the bladder at all times and off the floor**. Above the bladder, urine runs back up the tubing and seeds a catheter-associated infection; on the floor, the bag picks up organisms. Hang it on the bed frame, never the movable side rail, and empty it into a patient-specific graduate that never touches the drain spout.

For a clean-catch sample: cleanse front to back with the wipes, start the stream into the toilet, then catch the middle portion. The first part flushes urethral flora out of the way, which is the whole point.

### Stool

Report color, consistency, volume and frequency. **Black tarry stool (`melena`)** means digested blood from an upper GI bleed. **Bright red blood (`hematochezia`)** is lower, or upper and brisk. Clay-colored or pale stool suggests bile is not reaching the gut. Watery, foul, high-volume diarrhea in someone on antibiotics means `C. difficile` until proven otherwise — that patient goes on **contact precautions with soap-and-water hand washing**, because alcohol gel does not kill spores. Save the specimen; do not flush the evidence the team is about to order a test on.

### Emesis and drains

Emesis: volume, and whether it is bilious green, `coffee-ground` (old blood), bright red, or feculent. Measure it in the graduate, do not estimate from the emesis bag by eye.

Drains, nasogastric tubes, chest tubes and surgical drains: record output, color and whether it changed. A sudden increase in bright red from any drain gets called immediately. Chest tube systems stay **upright and below the chest** and are never clamped or lifted above the insertion site without an order.

### Ostomies

An `ileostomy` puts out `500 to 1000 mL` a day of thin, enzyme-rich liquid that burns skin quickly. A `colostomy` puts out thicker, more formed stool at lower volume. Empty the pouch when it is **one-third to one-half full** — heavier than that and the weight breaks the seal. The stoma itself should be beefy red and moist; **pale, dusky, purple or black is an emergency** and gets reported at once. A little bleeding when you clean it is normal; the stoma has no nerve endings, so pain is not your signal.

> **Key:** Measure, describe, then discard. Volume in milliliters, plus color, clarity and odor.

> **On shift:** A dusky stoma, output under 30 mL/hour, melena, or a chest tube suddenly filling with bright red blood are the four output findings you interrupt someone for.
keyPoints: Adult urine output 0.5 mL/kg/hour, about 30 to 50 mL/hour; under 30 mL/hour is oliguria and gets reported.
Catheter bag stays below the bladder, off the floor, hung on the frame not the side rail.
Melena is black and tarry from an upper GI bleed; coffee-ground emesis is old blood.
Suspected C. difficile means contact precautions and soap-and-water hand washing — alcohol gel does not kill spores.
Empty an ostomy pouch at one-third to one-half full; a pale, dusky or black stoma is an emergency.

checks.q: A 70 kg adult has produced 20 mL of urine in the last hour. What is this and what do you do?
choices: Normal output; chart it and move on
Oliguria; check the tubing for kinks and report it to the nurse now
Polyuria; push oral fluids
Expected after contrast; recheck in four hours
checks.why: Expected output is about 35 mL/hour for 70 kg. Under 30 mL/hour is oliguria and can signal shock, dehydration or obstruction — but a kinked or clamped catheter is a common mechanical cause worth ruling out first.

checks.q: A patient on antibiotics has high-volume, foul-smelling watery diarrhea. What hand hygiene applies?
choices: Alcohol-based hand rub is sufficient
Soap and water, because alcohol does not kill C. difficile spores
No hand hygiene needed if gloves were worn
Alcohol rub before and soap only at end of shift
checks.why: C. difficile spores survive alcohol; only the mechanical action of soap and running water removes them. Gloves reduce but do not eliminate hand contamination.

checks.q: You remove an ostomy pouch and the stoma is dusky purple. What does that mean?
choices: Normal variation in stoma color
Mild irritation from the adhesive
Compromised blood supply to the stoma — report immediately
Dehydration, which will resolve with fluids
checks.why: A healthy stoma is beefy red and moist. Pale, dusky, purple or black indicates ischemia or necrosis and is a surgical emergency, not a skin or hydration issue.

lessons.title: Mobility: gait belts, assist levels, and walking someone who might not make it
lessons.body:
Every hour a patient spends in bed costs strength. Older adults lose measurable muscle within days, and the first walk after a long stay is where a fall happens. Getting people up, safely, is prevention — but only if the assessment comes first.

### Before the feet hit the floor

Check four things: the **activity order** (bed rest, up with assist, up ad lib), what they can normally do at home, whether they are dizzy or medicated, and what is attached to them — IV lines, oxygen tubing, catheter bag, monitor leads, telemetry box. Sort the lines before you move, not during.

Non-skid footwear on both feet. Socks alone on a polished ED floor is a fall waiting to happen, and so is a gown untied and dragging.

### Dangle first

Sit them on the edge of the bed with feet flat on the floor for `1 to 2 minutes` before standing. This is not a courtesy. Standing suddenly after lying down drops blood pressure — `orthostatic hypotension`, defined as a fall of `20 mmHg systolic` or `10 mmHg diastolic` within 3 minutes of standing. Ask while they dangle: dizzy, lightheaded, nauseated, seeing gray? If yes, sit them back down. Do not talk them through it.

### The gait belt

Around the waist over clothing or a gown, snug enough that you can slide **only a flat hand** underneath, positioned below the ribs and above the hips. Never on bare skin, never over a fresh abdominal incision, ostomy, feeding tube, pacemaker site, or a pregnant abdomen — in those cases use a different technique or a lift.

Grip **underhand**, palms up, which is stronger and protects your wrist. Stand on the patient's **weaker side, slightly behind**, one hand in the belt and one near the shoulder. Count out loud: "On three — one, two, three, stand." Move with them, matching their pace.

A cane goes on the **strong** side and advances with the weak leg. A walker is advanced first, then the weak leg, then the strong leg, and the patient must never pull up on the walker to rise — they push off the bed or chair arms. For stairs, the phrase is **up with the good, down with the bad**: the strong leg leads going up, the weak leg leads coming down.

### If they start to go down

You do not catch them. Nobody catches an adult, and trying is how techs end up with a back injury and the patient lands worse.

Widen your stance, pull them **in toward your body**, and let them **slide down your leg** to the floor while you protect the head. Then stay with them and call for help. Do not lift them back up alone. Every fall gets reported, vitals rechecked, the nurse and the provider notified, and an event report filed — including a fall that hurt nobody.

> **Key:** Dangle 1 to 2 minutes, ask about dizziness, gait belt underhand, stand on the weak side, and slide rather than catch.

> **On shift:** Chart the distance and the assist level — `"ambulated 30 feet with a walker, one-person assist, steady, SpO2 94% on room air"`. That sentence is what a physical therapist and a discharge planner actually need.
keyPoints: Dangle at the edge of the bed 1 to 2 minutes and ask about dizziness before standing.
Orthostatic hypotension is a drop of 20 mmHg systolic or 10 mmHg diastolic within 3 minutes of standing.
Gait belt over clothing, one flat hand of slack, underhand grip, stand on the weaker side slightly behind.
Cane on the strong side; up with the good leg, down with the bad on stairs.
If a patient falls, do not catch — pull them in and slide them down your leg while protecting the head.

checks.q: Where do you stand when ambulating a patient who has left-sided weakness after a stroke?
choices: On the right side, directly in front
On the left side, slightly behind
Directly behind with both hands on the shoulders
On the right side, holding the right elbow
checks.why: You stand on the weaker side — here the left — slightly behind, so you can control a fall toward the side they are likely to fall. Standing in front blocks their path and gives you no leverage.

checks.q: A patient begins to collapse while you are walking her. What is correct?
choices: Catch her under the arms and hold her up until help arrives
Step away so she does not pull you down
Pull her in against your body and ease her down your leg to the floor, protecting her head
Lower her quickly and immediately lift her back into the wheelchair
checks.why: Controlled descent protects both of you. Catching causes back injuries and often a worse landing; stepping away lets her hit the floor unprotected; lifting her alone afterward risks a second injury before she is assessed.

checks.q: Which patient should not have a gait belt applied?
choices: A patient with a healed hip replacement from two years ago
A patient with a fresh abdominal incision
A patient with a peripheral IV in the left forearm
A patient wearing a hospital gown over a T-shirt
checks.why: A belt across a fresh abdominal wound, ostomy or feeding tube causes direct harm. An old hip replacement, a forearm IV and a gown are all compatible with normal belt use.

lessons.title: Transfers and fall prevention in an emergency department room
lessons.body:
Transfers are where techs get hurt and patients get dropped. Both outcomes come from the same two errors: guessing at how much the patient can help, and using arms instead of legs.

### Your body first

Feet shoulder-width apart, one foot slightly forward. **Bend the knees and hips, keep the back straight.** Hold the load close to your body — a weight held at arm's length multiplies the force on your lumbar spine several times over. **Pivot with your feet; never twist your torso.** Lead with the hips. Push and pull rather than lift whenever a surface allows it.

Raise the bed to **your hip height** before you work, and lower it after. Working at a low bed is the reason for half of the back injuries in the department.

Call for help by number, out loud: "I need two more for a lateral transfer." The safe manual-lift limit commonly taught is about `35 pounds` of patient weight per person; beyond that you use a mechanical lift, a friction-reducing slide sheet, or an air transfer mattress. There is no award for doing it alone.

### Bed to stretcher, and bed to chair

**Lateral transfer (bed to stretcher):** surfaces level and locked, slide sheet or transfer board under the patient, one person at the head managing the airway and lines, the counter calls the move, and everyone **pulls on the sheet** on "three" — nobody lifts.

**Pivot transfer (bed to wheelchair):** chair on the patient's **strong side**, angled about `45 degrees` to the bed, **wheels locked**, footrests removed or swung away. Patient dangles, then stands with the gait belt, pivots on their feet in small steps, feels the chair against the back of their legs, reaches back for the armrests, and sits. Your knee blocks their weak knee. Nobody is lifted under the armpits — that dislocates shoulders and tears rotator cuffs.

### Falls: the highest-volume harm in the department

ED falls happen in predictable places: getting off a stretcher unassisted, in the bathroom, and while reaching for something out of range.

The interventions are boring and they work:

- **Bed in the lowest position, wheels locked**, always, every time you leave the room.
- **Call bell, phone, water, urinal and glasses within reach** before you walk out. Most falls begin with a patient reaching.
- **Two side rails up** is standard positioning. All four rails up is a **restraint** — it traps the patient, who then climbs over the end, which is worse than any fall from bed height.
- Non-skid footwear on, floor dry, clutter and cords out of the walking path.
- **Never leave a high-risk patient alone in a bathroom.** Stay outside the door, talking.
- Toilet on a schedule, roughly every 2 hours; unmet toileting need is the leading trigger.
- Honor the fall-risk identifiers your facility uses — a colored wristband, a magnet or sign, yellow socks — and know that a patient with dementia, on sedatives, or previously fallen is in that group regardless of what they tell you.

> **Trap:** "I'll be right back" while the bed is high and the rails are down. That sentence precedes a huge number of ED falls.

> **On shift:** Hourly rounding scripted around the four P's — **pain, potty, position, possessions** — measurably reduces falls and call bell use. Say all four out loud each round.
keyPoints: Bend knees and hips, load close, pivot with the feet, never twist; raise the bed to your hip height to work.
Beyond roughly 35 pounds of patient weight per person, use a lift, slide sheet or air mattress and more people.
Lateral transfers are pulled on a slide sheet by a counted team with one person managing the head and lines.
Wheelchair on the strong side at 45 degrees, wheels locked, footrests off; never lift under the armpits.
Bed low and locked, call bell in reach, two rails up — four rails up is a restraint.

checks.q: You raise all four side rails on a confused patient to keep him in bed. What have you done?
choices: Applied a standard safety measure
Applied a physical restraint that requires an order and monitoring
Reduced fall risk with no downside
Complied with a universal fall precaution
checks.why: Four rails up prevents voluntary exit and meets the definition of a physical restraint. It also raises the height a determined patient falls from when he climbs over the foot of the bed.

checks.q: How is a wheelchair positioned for a pivot transfer from a bed?
choices: On the weak side, parallel to the bed, brakes off so it can be adjusted
On the strong side, about 45 degrees to the bed, wheels locked, footrests swung away
Directly facing the bed with the footrests down for support
Behind the patient so they can back into it blindly
checks.why: Pivoting toward the strong side uses the leg that works, the angle shortens the turn, locked wheels stop the chair sliding, and footrests left down are a tripping and shearing hazard.

checks.q: Which set of actions is the four P's of hourly rounding?
choices: Pulse, pressure, pupils, pain
Pain, potty, position, possessions
Privacy, permission, procedure, paperwork
Position, perfusion, pallor, pain
checks.why: Pain, potty, position and possessions address the four reasons patients get up or press the call bell. The others describe assessment findings, not a rounding script.

lessons.title: Comfort, dying, and the conversation you are actually able to have
lessons.body:
People die in emergency departments, and often the tech is the person in the room. This is a skill like any other and it has specific moves.

### Comfort is measurable work

Warm blankets. The head of the bed at the angle they ask for. Lights down, door closed, the monitor volume lowered if the nurse agrees. A pillow under an arm that has been dependent for hours. Dry linen. An offer of a urinal before the family arrives. Mouth care for someone who is NPO and parched — a moist swab, not water.

Ask about pain in numbers and pass it on immediately: `0 to 10` for adults who can answer, and the `Wong-Baker faces` scale for children `3 years and up`. For a patient who cannot report — advanced dementia, intubated, nonverbal — you watch behavior: grimacing, restlessness, guarding, a rising heart rate, moaning on movement. Report what you saw, not a number you invented. **Untreated pain is the most common thing a tech is positioned to notice and the nurse is not.**

### Code status in plain words

`Full code` means everything: compressions, defibrillation, drugs, intubation. `DNR` means no compressions and no shocks if the heart stops. `DNI` means no breathing tube. `DNR/DNI` can still receive antibiotics, fluids, oxygen and pain medicine — **DNR is not "do not treat."** A `POLST` or `MOLST` form is a signed physician order that travels with the patient and is honored; an advance directive or living will is the patient's stated wish and needs a clinician to act on it. `Comfort measures only` means the plan is symptom relief.

If a patient or a family member asks you what any of this means, you can define the terms. You do not have the goals-of-care conversation. You get the nurse or the physician.

### Being there

Sit down. A seated visitor is perceived as having stayed far longer than a standing one. Match their volume. Silence is allowed — do not fill it.

Do not say "I know how you feel," "he's in a better place," "at least she didn't suffer," or "everything happens for a reason." Say: "I'm sorry." "I'm here." "Take whatever time you need." "Would you like me to get the chaplain?" Offer water, tissues, a chair, and a phone.

### After a death

Ask the nurse first whether the case is a **medical examiner case** — unexpected, traumatic, in custody, suspicious, or within a certain window of admission. In an ME case **nothing is removed**: no lines, no tubes, no endotracheal tube, no clothing. Leave everything in place.

Otherwise, postmortem care is done before rigor mortis begins in `2 to 4 hours`: wash the body, close the eyes and mouth, remove lines if permitted, place absorbent pads, put dentures in, straighten the limbs and raise the head of the bed slightly to keep blood from pooling in the face. Handle the body gently — the family may walk in, and someone is always watching.

Before viewing: dim the lights, clean visible blood, cover the body to the shoulders with a clean sheet, and give the family unlimited time. Inventory and bag valuables **with a second person witnessing**, and document it. Offer a lock of hair, handprints or footprints for a child; those offers are made once, gently, and never pushed.

> **Key:** In a medical examiner case, every tube, line and item of clothing stays exactly where it is.

> **On shift:** Tell the charge nurse if a death hit you. Debriefs and peer support exist for staff, and the techs who last in this job are the ones who use them.
keyPoints: DNR means no compressions and no shocks — it is not 'do not treat'; DNI means no breathing tube.
A POLST or MOLST is a signed physician order that travels with the patient; a living will is a stated wish.
For nonverbal patients, report observed pain behavior — grimacing, guarding, restlessness — not an invented number.
In a medical examiner case, leave all tubes, lines and clothing in place.
Postmortem care happens before rigor mortis at 2 to 4 hours; valuables are bagged and documented with a witness.

checks.q: A family asks whether their father's DNR order means he will stop getting antibiotics and oxygen. What is accurate?
choices: Yes, DNR means all treatment stops
No — DNR limits compressions and shocks; antibiotics, oxygen, fluids and pain medicine continue unless separately limited
Yes, but only after the attending signs a second form
DNR only applies once the patient is unconscious
checks.why: DNR addresses what happens at cardiac arrest. It does not withdraw ongoing treatment. Comfort-measures-only is the separate order that narrows care to symptom relief.

checks.q: A patient dies and the nurse tells you it is a medical examiner case. What do you do with the endotracheal tube and IV lines?
choices: Remove them and bag them for the family
Remove the IVs but leave the tube
Leave everything in place, including clothing
Remove everything and clean the body for viewing
checks.why: In an ME case the body and all devices are evidence and stay untouched until the examiner releases them. Removing anything can destroy the record of how the patient was treated and how they died.

checks.q: A nonverbal patient with advanced dementia grimaces and guards her abdomen whenever you reposition her. How should you report it?
choices: "Pain 8 out of 10"
"No complaints of pain"
"Grimacing and guarding the abdomen with movement, heart rate up to 104"
"Appears comfortable at rest so no report needed"
checks.why: You report observed behavior and objective data. Assigning a number she did not give fabricates a finding, and 'no complaints' from a patient who cannot complain hides real pain.

cards.front: What four moves open every hands-on task with a patient?
cards.back: Knock and announce yourself, explain in one plain sentence what and why, ask permission and offer a choice, then close the curtain and cover everything you are not working on.

cards.front: A competent patient refuses care you were told to do. What is the correct response?
cards.back: Accept it, find out the concern, and report it to the nurse. A refusal is a legal right and clinical information; proceeding anyway is battery.

cards.front: Which kinds of care require a documented chaperone?
cards.back: Anything involving genitals, breasts or rectum. The chaperone's name goes in the chart — it protects the patient and you.

cards.front: Which words replace 'diaper', 'potty' and 'sweetie' in an adult room?
cards.back: Brief, bedpan, and the patient's own name with a title until they say otherwise.

cards.front: Why do you speak to a sedated or intubated patient as if they hear you?
cards.back: Because they often do. Hearing is the last sense to fade, and families in the doorway are listening too.

cards.front: What water temperature is used for a bed bath?
cards.back: About 105 to 110 F (41 to 43 C). Test it on the inside of your wrist — never rely on a neuropathic or confused patient's report.

cards.front: In what order is a bed bath performed, and why?
cards.back: Clean to dirty, top to bottom: eyes, face, arms, chest, abdomen, legs, back, perineum last. Folds and perineum carry the heaviest bacterial load.

cards.front: How is female perineal care performed?
cards.back: Separate the labia and wipe front to back, one downward stroke per fresh cloth surface. Back to front drags bowel flora into the urethra.

cards.front: What step must never be skipped when cleaning an uncircumcised male?
cards.back: Replacing the foreskin after cleaning. Left retracted, it swells and can strangle the glans — paraphimosis.

cards.front: How do you position an unconscious patient for oral care?
cards.back: Head of bed elevated if allowed, head turned to the side, suction at the bedside, minimally moist swab or brush, and no free water in the mouth.

cards.front: Where do dentures go when they come out?
cards.back: In a denture cup labeled with the patient's name. Wrapped in a napkin is how they end up in the trash and on an incident report.

cards.front: Why are skin folds and spaces between the toes dried carefully?
cards.back: Trapped moisture macerates skin and lets it break down within a day, especially under breasts, in the groin and under an abdominal pannus.

cards.front: How often should toileting be offered to prevent falls?
cards.back: About every 2 hours while awake. Unmet toileting need is the leading reason patients get up alone and fall.

cards.front: Which patients get a fracture pan, and which way does it face?
cards.back: Hip fracture, spinal precautions, post-op hip, or anyone who cannot lift the pelvis. The shallow tapered end slides under the buttocks toward the head of the bed.

cards.front: What head-of-bed angle is used for a bedpan, and why?
cards.back: About 30 to 45 degrees if the condition allows. Nobody can defecate flat on their back; the position opens the anorectal angle.

cards.front: How long can a patient safely remain on a bedpan?
cards.back: No more than about 5 minutes before you check. Longer concentrates pressure on the sacrum and causes skin injury.

cards.front: What is incontinence-associated dermatitis and how is it treated?
cards.back: A chemical, moisture-driven skin breakdown from urine or stool. Clean promptly with a pH-balanced cleanser, pat dry, and apply a zinc oxide or dimethicone barrier.

cards.front: Why is a brief a last resort rather than a default?
cards.back: Placing a continent adult in a brief teaches learned incontinence and adds a moisture injury risk. If a patient in one is continent, say so.

cards.front: Why is a bed made one whole side at a time?
cards.back: Completing the bottom sheet, draw sheet and top linen on one side before walking around halves the steps. Going back and forth is the main reason people are slow.

cards.front: Why must the bottom sheet be taut?
cards.back: A wrinkle under the sacrum concentrates pressure into a line. During a long boarding stay that line becomes a pressure injury.

cards.front: Where does a draw or slide sheet sit, and what is it for?
cards.back: From the shoulders to mid-thigh, under the torso and pelvis. It is the tool you use to boost, turn and lateral-transfer.

cards.front: Name three things you never do with linen.
cards.back: Never shake it, never put it on the floor, and never hold soiled linen against your uniform. Shaking aerosolizes skin cells and C. difficile spores.

cards.front: What happens to unused clean linen brought into a patient room?
cards.back: It is discarded or laundered. Anything that crosses into the patient zone is contaminated and does not return to the warmer or the clean cart.

cards.front: How is an occupied bed changed?
cards.back: Roll the patient away from you with the far rail up, fan-fold soiled linen against their back, lay clean linen on the empty half, then roll them over the ridge from the other side. Two people is standard.

cards.front: How long does unrelieved pressure take to start damaging tissue?
cards.back: 1 to 2 hours. Muscle dies before skin does, so the visible mark is the small end of a larger cone of dead tissue.

cards.front: How do you test for a stage 1 pressure injury?
cards.back: Press the red area for about 3 seconds and release. If it blanches white and re-pinks, flow is intact. If it stays red, it is a stage 1 injury.

cards.front: What distinguishes a stage 3 from a stage 4 pressure injury?
cards.back: Stage 3 is full thickness with fat visible. Stage 4 exposes bone, tendon or muscle.

cards.front: What does deep purple or maroon intact skin over a bony prominence mean?
cards.back: A deep tissue pressure injury — damage that started in the muscle underneath and is working its way out. Report it as a pressure injury.

cards.front: What does 'unstageable' mean?
cards.back: The wound base is covered by slough or eschar, so the depth cannot be judged. It is full thickness, but the stage cannot be assigned until the base is visible.

cards.front: How often is a patient repositioned in bed and in a chair?
cards.back: At least every 2 hours in bed and every 1 hour in a chair — or a weight shift every 15 minutes if they can do it themselves.

cards.front: How are heels offloaded correctly?
cards.back: A pillow lengthwise under the calves so the heels float free of the bed. A pillow under the heels merely relocates the pressure.

cards.front: Why is a 30-degree lateral tilt preferred over full side-lying?
cards.back: A 90-degree side-lying position loads the greater trochanter directly. A 30-degree tilt spreads the load across the buttock instead.

cards.front: Why should you never massage a reddened bony prominence or use a donut cushion?
cards.back: Massage shears already-damaged capillaries. A donut creates a ring of ischemia around the very area it is supposed to protect.

cards.front: What is shear, and how do you avoid it?
cards.back: Tissue layers sliding against each other under intact skin, which tears blood supply. Avoid it by lifting or sliding on a sheet rather than dragging.

cards.front: Name four device-related pressure injury sites a tech creates.
cards.back: Under oxygen tubing over the ear, under a pulse oximeter probe left on one finger, under a cervical collar, and at the nares from a nasal cannula.

cards.front: Does NPO include ice chips?
cards.back: Yes. An ice chip is water, and thin water is the highest-risk consistency for someone with an unscreened swallow.

cards.front: What must happen before a new stroke patient's first sip?
cards.back: A bedside swallow screen performed by the nurse or speech-language pathology. A tech does not clear a swallow.

cards.front: What position and head angle are used for feeding?
cards.back: Fully upright at 90 degrees with the chin tucked slightly toward the chest. Never tip the head back — that opens the airway to the bolus.

cards.front: How long does a patient stay upright after a meal?
cards.back: 30 to 60 minutes. Lying down soon after eating lets reflux reach the airway.

cards.front: Why are straws avoided in aspiration-risk patients?
cards.back: A straw delivers a fast bolus to the back of the throat, ahead of the swallow reflex, which is exactly the timing problem these patients have.

cards.front: What are the thickened liquid consistencies you will hear ordered?
cards.back: Nectar, honey and pudding thick. Thicker liquids move slowly enough for a delayed swallow reflex to close the airway in time.

cards.front: Which signs during a meal mean stop and call the nurse?
cards.back: Coughing or throat clearing, a wet or gurgly voice, drooling, pocketing food, watering eyes, a change in breathing, or a falling SpO2.

cards.front: What is silent aspiration?
cards.back: Material entering the airway without any cough. Up to half of stroke patients who aspirate never cough, which is why absence of coughing proves nothing.

cards.front: How is intake documented after a meal?
cards.back: Percentage of the tray eaten and fluid volume in milliliters, such as 'ate 50% of tray, 240 mL apple juice'. 'Tolerated diet' is not documentation.

cards.front: What is normal adult urine output, and what number triggers a report?
cards.back: About 0.5 mL/kg/hour, roughly 30 to 50 mL/hour. Under 30 mL/hour in an adult is oliguria and gets reported.

cards.front: A catheter has drained nothing in two hours. What do you check before calling it renal failure?
cards.back: The tubing — kinks, clamps, dependent loops, the patient lying on it, and the bag position. Mechanical obstruction is common.

cards.front: Where must a urinary drainage bag hang?
cards.back: Below the level of the bladder, off the floor, on the bed frame rather than a movable side rail. Above the bladder, urine refluxes and seeds infection.

cards.front: How is a clean-catch midstream sample collected?
cards.back: Cleanse front to back with the provided wipes, start the stream into the toilet, then catch the middle portion. The first part flushes urethral flora away.

cards.front: What does black tarry stool mean?
cards.back: Melena — digested blood, usually from an upper GI bleed. Bright red blood per rectum is hematochezia, a lower source or a brisk upper one.

cards.front: What hand hygiene is required for suspected C. difficile, and why?
cards.back: Soap and water. Alcohol-based rub does not kill spores; only the mechanical action of washing removes them.

cards.front: What does coffee-ground emesis indicate?
cards.back: Old blood partially digested by stomach acid, pointing to upper GI bleeding. Bright red emesis is active bleeding; green is bilious.

cards.front: At what fullness is an ostomy pouch emptied, and why?
cards.back: One-third to one-half full. Beyond that, the weight of the contents pulls the wafer off and breaks the seal.

cards.front: What color should a stoma be, and what color is an emergency?
cards.back: Beefy red and moist is healthy. Pale, dusky, purple or black means the blood supply is compromised and is reported immediately.

cards.front: How much does an ileostomy typically put out in a day, compared with a colostomy?
cards.back: An ileostomy drains about 500 to 1000 mL of thin, enzyme-rich liquid that burns skin. A colostomy puts out thicker, more formed stool at lower volume.

cards.front: How long should a patient dangle before standing, and what do you ask?
cards.back: 1 to 2 minutes with feet flat on the floor. Ask about dizziness, lightheadedness, nausea or gray vision, and sit them back if any is present.

cards.front: Define orthostatic hypotension in numbers.
cards.back: A drop of 20 mmHg systolic or 10 mmHg diastolic within 3 minutes of standing from a lying or sitting position.

cards.front: How tight is a gait belt, and where does it go?
cards.back: Over clothing, below the ribs and above the hips, snug enough that only a flat hand slides underneath. Never on bare skin.

cards.front: Which patients should not get a gait belt?
cards.back: Fresh abdominal incision, ostomy, feeding tube, recently placed pacemaker, or a pregnant abdomen. Use another technique or a mechanical lift.

cards.front: Where do you stand and how do you grip when ambulating a patient?
cards.back: On the weaker side, slightly behind, with an underhand palms-up grip on the belt and one hand near the shoulder.

cards.front: Which side does a cane go on, and what is the stair rule?
cards.back: The cane goes on the strong side and advances with the weak leg. On stairs: up with the good leg, down with the bad.

cards.front: What do you do when a patient starts to fall while you are walking them?
cards.back: Do not catch. Widen your stance, pull them in against your body, and let them slide down your leg to the floor while protecting the head. Then call for help.

cards.front: What does good ambulation charting look like?
cards.back: Distance, device, assist level, steadiness and any vitals — for example 'ambulated 30 feet with a walker, one-person assist, steady, SpO2 94% on room air'.

cards.front: What is the rough manual lift limit per person before you use equipment?
cards.back: About 35 pounds of patient weight per caregiver. Beyond that, use a slide sheet, an air transfer mattress or a mechanical lift and more people.

cards.front: At what height should the bed be while you work, and where is it left?
cards.back: Raised to your hip height while you work; returned to the lowest position with wheels locked before you leave the room.

cards.front: How is a lateral bed-to-stretcher transfer performed?
cards.back: Surfaces level and locked, slide sheet or board under the patient, one person at the head managing airway and lines, and the team pulls on a count. Nobody lifts.

cards.front: How is a wheelchair set up for a pivot transfer?
cards.back: On the patient's strong side at about 45 degrees to the bed, wheels locked, footrests removed or swung away.

cards.front: Why is lifting a patient under the armpits forbidden?
cards.back: It dislocates shoulders and tears rotator cuffs. Use a gait belt and let the patient bear weight through their own legs.

cards.front: How many side rails up is standard, and what does all four mean?
cards.back: Two is standard positioning. All four up prevents voluntary exit and counts as a physical restraint, requiring an order and monitoring.

cards.front: What are the four P's of hourly rounding?
cards.back: Pain, potty, position, possessions. Saying all four out loud each round measurably reduces falls and call bell use.

cards.front: What does DNR actually restrict, and what does it not?
cards.back: It restricts chest compressions and defibrillation at cardiac arrest. It does not stop antibiotics, fluids, oxygen or pain medicine. DNI separately means no breathing tube.

cards.front: What is the difference between a POLST/MOLST and a living will?
cards.back: A POLST or MOLST is a signed physician order that travels with the patient and is acted on directly. A living will states the patient's wishes and needs a clinician to translate it into orders.

cards.front: Which pain scales apply to adults and to young children?
cards.back: A 0 to 10 numeric scale for adults who can answer; the Wong-Baker faces scale for children roughly 3 years and older.

cards.front: How do you report pain in a patient who cannot speak?
cards.back: Describe observed behavior — grimacing, guarding, restlessness, moaning on movement, a rising heart rate. Do not invent a number they did not give.

cards.front: What is removed from the body in a medical examiner case?
cards.back: Nothing. Tubes, lines, the endotracheal tube and clothing all stay exactly in place until the examiner releases the body.

cards.front: Why is postmortem care done within 2 to 4 hours?
cards.back: Rigor mortis begins in that window. After it sets, the eyes and mouth cannot be closed and the limbs cannot be straightened for the family's viewing.

quiz.q: A tech is about to change a patient's brief. Which opening is correct?
choices: Say her name, explain the task in one sentence, ask if now is okay, then close the curtain and cover what is not being cleaned
Pull the curtain and begin, since the patient is confused
Ask the family to step out and start without speaking
Announce the task to the nurse across the room first
quiz.why: Announce, explain, ask, cover. Confusion does not remove the requirement to explain — it increases it, because an unexplained touch is what triggers combativeness. Speaking about the patient across the room violates privacy.

quiz.q: A male patient repeatedly makes sexual comments while you take his vital signs. What is the correct response?
choices: State the boundary once in a flat voice, leave the room, and tell the charge nurse
Laugh it off to keep the interaction light
Finish the vitals quickly and say nothing
Ask a coworker to take over without explaining why
quiz.why: One flat boundary statement, exit, and report. Laughing signals the behavior is acceptable, saying nothing leaves the next staff member unwarned, and silently handing the patient off puts a colleague into the same situation blind.

quiz.q: During a bed bath you find a non-blanchable red area over the sacrum of a nursing home patient who arrived two hours ago. What matters most?
choices: Documenting and reporting it now, because an injury present on arrival must be attributed correctly
Applying lotion and massaging the area to restore circulation
Waiting until the patient is admitted so the floor nurse can assess it
Covering it with a dressing before anyone else sees it
quiz.why: Charting it in the ED establishes that it was present on arrival, which matters clinically and medicolegally. Massage shears damaged capillaries, delay transfers responsibility to your hospital, and covering it hides the finding.

quiz.q: You are washing a patient's face, arms and chest. Which cloth surface may be reused for the perineum?
choices: Any surface, since the same basin water is used throughout
A surface used on the legs only
None — the perineum is washed last with fresh surfaces
A surface used on the face, since the face is cleanest
quiz.why: Clean to dirty runs one direction only. Nothing used on cleaner skin is carried down to the perineum, and nothing that has touched the perineum goes back. Fresh surfaces for the highest-load area protect everything already cleaned.

quiz.q: A tech retracts an uncircumcised patient's foreskin to clean the glans and is called away urgently. Two hours later the glans is swollen and painful. What happened?
choices: Paraphimosis from a foreskin left retracted
Cellulitis from inadequate cleaning
An allergic reaction to the soap
A normal finding after peri care
quiz.why: A retracted foreskin acts as a constricting band, causing venous congestion and swelling. Cellulitis develops over days with warmth and erythema, and an allergic reaction would itch and involve a wider area.

quiz.q: Which patient most needs a fracture pan rather than a standard bedpan?
choices: A 78-year-old with a suspected hip fracture who cannot lift her pelvis
A 30-year-old with a wrist fracture
A 55-year-old with abdominal pain who can sit up freely
A 40-year-old on a cardiac monitor who ambulates
quiz.why: The fracture pan exists for patients who cannot raise the pelvis. A wrist fracture, free mobility, and monitored ambulation all allow a standard pan or the bathroom.

quiz.q: A tech places a confused 85-year-old on a bedpan, closes the curtain, and returns 20 minutes later. What is the primary harm?
choices: Sacral pressure injury and an unwitnessed fall risk
Delayed specimen collection
Loss of patient dignity only
Inaccurate intake and output
quiz.why: Prolonged bedpan contact concentrates pressure on the sacrum, and a confused patient left alone may try to get off the pan and fall. Dignity and documentation matter but are not the physical harm here.

quiz.q: Why is a bed's bottom sheet smoothed rather than left loose?
choices: A wrinkle under a bony prominence concentrates pressure and can cause a pressure injury
Loose linen violates infection control policy
It makes the bed easier to strip later
Tight linen keeps the patient warmer
quiz.why: Pressure injury is about force per unit area; a fold turns diffuse pressure into a line. The other options are cosmetic or unrelated to tissue perfusion.

quiz.q: A tech strips a bed and shakes out the sheet before bagging it. What risk has been created?
choices: Skin cells and spores including C. difficile have been aerosolized into the room
The linen is now unusable and must be discarded
The patient's belongings may have been thrown to the floor
None, as long as gloves were worn
quiz.why: Shaking launches contaminated particles onto every surface and into the air. Gloves protect the hands, not the room, and the linen was headed to the laundry regardless.

quiz.q: A supine patient's heels are reddened. Which intervention is correct?
choices: A donut cushion under each heel
A pillow placed directly beneath the heels
A pillow lengthwise under the calves so the heels float
Vigorous massage every two hours
quiz.why: Floating the heels removes contact entirely. A pillow under the heels shifts but does not remove pressure, a donut creates circumferential ischemia, and massage damages compromised capillaries.

quiz.q: A sacral wound shows visible subcutaneous fat but no bone, tendon or muscle, and the base is clearly seen. What stage is this?
choices: Stage 3
Stage 2
Stage 4
Unstageable
quiz.why: Full thickness with fat visible and no deeper structures exposed is stage 3. Stage 2 has no fat visible, stage 4 exposes bone, tendon or muscle, and unstageable means slough or eschar hides the base.

quiz.q: A patient boarding for nine hours has a pulse oximeter probe left on the same finger the entire time. What is the risk?
choices: Falsely high saturation readings only
Nerve damage to the brachial plexus
Hemolysis of capillary blood
A device-related pressure injury at the probe site
quiz.why: Continuous probe pressure on one digit causes a device-related pressure injury, which is why probes are rotated on a schedule. Readings may drift, but the tissue injury is the harm being prevented.

quiz.q: A patient has been side-lying at a full 90 degrees for three hours. Which site is at greatest risk?
choices: The sacrum
The occiput
The ischial tuberosities
The greater trochanter
quiz.why: Full side-lying loads the trochanter directly, which is why a 30-degree tilt is preferred. The sacrum and occiput load in the supine position and the ischial tuberosities load in sitting.

quiz.q: A new stroke patient asks for water. There is no swallow screen documented. What do you do?
choices: Give a small sip of water only
Give ice chips instead, which are safer
Keep her NPO and tell the nurse she is thirsty and needs a swallow screen
Offer thickened liquid from the pantry
quiz.why: Thin liquids including melted ice are the highest-risk consistency, and choosing a thickened substitute yourself is making a diet decision outside your scope. The right move is to report the need for a screen.

quiz.q: During feeding, a patient's voice becomes wet and gurgly and her SpO2 falls from 97% to 91%. What is your first action?
choices: Give a sip of water to clear the throat
Lower the head of the bed and turn her head
Continue but switch to thickened liquids
Stop the feeding, keep her fully upright, and get the nurse
quiz.why: A wet voice with desaturation is aspiration until proven otherwise. Stopping and staying upright protects the airway. Water adds volume, lowering the bed removes gravity protection, and changing consistency is a clinician's decision.

quiz.q: Why does a chin tuck reduce aspiration risk?
choices: It slows the rate at which the patient eats
It stimulates the gag reflex
It increases saliva production
It narrows the laryngeal opening and widens the food path behind it
quiz.why: Flexing the neck mechanically protects the airway entrance during the swallow. Extending the neck does the opposite. The chin tuck is a position, not a pacing or reflex technique.

quiz.q: A post-stroke patient eats an entire meal with no coughing at all. Is aspiration excluded?
choices: Yes, an intact cough reflex rules it out
Yes, provided her SpO2 stayed above 95%
No — silent aspiration occurs in a large share of stroke patients
No, but only if she has a tracheostomy
quiz.why: Up to half of stroke patients who aspirate do so silently, without any cough. That is precisely why a formal swallow screen exists rather than watching for coughing.

quiz.q: A 60 kg adult has produced 25 mL of urine over the past hour. How do you interpret this?
choices: Normal for this weight
Polyuria requiring fluid restriction
Unable to interpret without a 24-hour collection
Oliguria — expected output is about 30 mL/hour
quiz.why: At 0.5 mL/kg/hour, a 60 kg adult should make about 30 mL/hour. Twenty-five is below threshold and is reported. Polyuria is excessive output, and a single low hour is actionable without a 24-hour collection.

quiz.q: A transporter hangs a urinary drainage bag on the side rail during a move, and it ends up above the level of the bladder. What is the risk?
choices: The bag will overfill
The catheter balloon will deflate
The output measurement will read falsely high
Urine refluxes up the tubing and raises the risk of a catheter-associated urinary tract infection
quiz.why: Gravity is the only thing keeping the system one-directional. A bag above the bladder lets colonized urine run back into it. Balloon deflation and volume errors are unrelated to bag height.

quiz.q: A patient on antibiotics for a week has profuse, foul, watery diarrhea. Which combination is correct?
choices: Contact precautions and alcohol-based hand rub
Droplet precautions and soap-and-water hand washing
Contact precautions and soap-and-water hand washing
Standard precautions only, since diarrhea is not airborne
quiz.why: Suspected C. difficile requires contact precautions, and alcohol does not kill the spores — only soap and running water removes them mechanically. Droplet precautions apply to respiratory spread.

quiz.q: You remove an ostomy appliance and the stoma is pale and dusky rather than beefy red. What does this require?
choices: Routine pouch replacement and documentation at end of shift
Application of a barrier ring and reassessment tomorrow
Extra oral fluids to improve perfusion
Immediate report — the stoma's blood supply may be compromised
quiz.why: A dusky stoma indicates ischemia and possible necrosis, which is a surgical emergency. Routine documentation, barrier products and oral fluids all delay recognition of a vascular problem.

quiz.q: Which emesis description most suggests bleeding that has been present for some time rather than active hemorrhage?
choices: Bright red blood
Green bilious fluid
Clear frothy liquid
Coffee-ground material
quiz.why: Coffee-ground emesis is blood partially digested by acid, meaning it has sat in the stomach. Bright red is active bleeding, green is bile, and clear frothy fluid is neither.

quiz.q: A patient has been lying flat for six hours and you are getting her up. What is the first step after checking the activity order?
choices: Stand her with a gait belt immediately
Dangle her at the edge of the bed for 1 to 2 minutes and ask about dizziness
Take a blood pressure while supine only
Place her directly in a wheelchair using a two-person lift
quiz.why: Dangling allows the baroreceptor response to catch up after prolonged recumbency. Standing immediately invites orthostatic syncope, and lifting her skips the assessment that tells you whether she can bear weight at all.

quiz.q: A patient's blood pressure is 128/76 lying and 104/64 standing after two minutes. What does this indicate?
choices: A normal physiologic response
Orthostatic hypotension by the systolic criterion
Orthostatic hypotension by the diastolic criterion only
Hypertensive urgency
quiz.why: The systolic dropped 24 mmHg, exceeding the 20 mmHg threshold within 3 minutes. The diastolic fell only 12 mmHg, which alone would also meet the 10 mmHg criterion, but the systolic is the clearer finding here and nothing about this is hypertensive.

quiz.q: Which patient may not have a gait belt applied around the waist?
choices: A patient with chronic knee osteoarthritis
A patient with a colostomy and a fresh abdominal incision
A patient with an IV in the antecubital fossa
A patient wearing a telemetry box clipped to the gown
quiz.why: A belt across an ostomy or a fresh incision causes direct injury. Knee arthritis, a forearm or antecubital IV, and a telemetry box are all compatible with normal gait belt use.

quiz.q: A patient using a walker begins to pull himself up by the walker frame to stand. What should you do?
choices: Allow it if he does it at home
Steady the walker and let him continue
Stop him and have him push off the bed or chair arms, then grasp the walker once standing
Replace the walker with a cane
