quiz.why: Pulling on a walker tips it forward and is a common fall mechanism. The correct sequence is to push up from a fixed surface, then take the walker. Substituting a cane is a therapy decision, not a fix for technique.

quiz.q: A patient's knees buckle mid-hallway. What is the safest action?
choices: Catch her under the arms and hold her upright
Pull her toward your body and ease her down your leg to the floor, protecting her head
Step back and let her fall clear of you
Grab the gait belt with one hand and call for help before doing anything else
quiz.why: Controlled descent protects the patient's head and your spine. Catching causes caregiver back injury and shoulder trauma, stepping away leaves her unprotected, and waiting to act before controlling the descent wastes the only seconds available.

quiz.q: You need to move a 260-pound patient from bed to stretcher. What is the correct approach?
choices: Two staff lifting on the draw sheet
One staff at the head and one at the feet, lifting on a count
A team using a slide sheet or air transfer mattress, surfaces level and locked, with one person controlling the head and lines
Have the patient scoot over unassisted to avoid staff injury
quiz.why: Above roughly 35 pounds of weight per person, equipment replaces muscle. A friction-reducing device with a counted team pull is the standard. Two-person lifts of this weight injure staff, and an unassisted scoot risks the patient falling between surfaces.

quiz.q: Before leaving any patient room, which set is required?
choices: Bed in the lowest position, wheels locked, call bell and possessions in reach
All four side rails up and the door closed
Bed raised to hip height so the next staff member can work
Bed flat with the patient's shoes removed
quiz.why: Low, locked, and everything within reach addresses the actual fall mechanisms. Four rails up is a restraint, a raised bed increases fall height, and removing shoes makes any attempted ambulation less safe.

quiz.q: A confused patient repeatedly tries to climb out of bed. A tech raises all four side rails. What is the best assessment of this action?
choices: An appropriate and standard fall precaution
A physical restraint that requires an order, and one that increases the height of a fall
Acceptable as long as the bed is in the lowest position
Required by policy for all confused patients
quiz.why: Four rails prevent voluntary exit, which is the definition of a physical restraint. The determined patient then goes over the foot of the bed from a greater height. Bed height does not change the restraint classification.

quiz.q: How should you pivot while moving a patient from bed to chair?
choices: Twist at the waist while keeping the feet planted
Step and turn with your feet, keeping shoulders and hips aligned
Lean forward from the hips with straight legs
Reach across the bed and pull toward you
quiz.why: Rotational load on a flexed lumbar spine is the classic mechanism of caregiver back injury. Moving the feet keeps the spine in a neutral, stacked position. Straight-leg leaning and long reaches both multiply lumbar force.

quiz.q: A family member asks whether their mother's DNR means she cannot receive antibiotics for her pneumonia. What is the accurate answer?
choices: Correct, DNR withdraws all active treatment
DNR limits resuscitation at cardiac arrest; antibiotics, oxygen, fluids and pain medicine continue unless separately limited
DNR only applies outside the hospital
The tech should decline to answer and say nothing
quiz.why: DNR governs what happens at arrest, not ongoing treatment. Comfort-measures-only is the separate order that narrows care. A tech may accurately define terms; what a tech does not do is lead a goals-of-care discussion.

quiz.q: A patient dies unexpectedly in the ED and the case is referred to the medical examiner. What is correct?
choices: Remove all lines and tubes and clean the body for the family
Remove the endotracheal tube only, since it is distressing to see
Leave all tubes, lines and clothing in place
Remove clothing and bag it separately for the family
quiz.why: In an ME case every device and item of clothing is part of the record of the death and the resuscitation. Removing anything, even for kindness, destroys evidence and can compromise the investigation.

quiz.q: Which statement to a grieving family is appropriate?
choices: "I know exactly how you feel."
"At least she didn't suffer."
"I'm sorry. Take whatever time you need. Would you like me to get the chaplain?"
"Everything happens for a reason."
quiz.why: Acknowledgment, permission to take time, and a concrete offer of support are what help. The other three claim an experience you do not have, minimize the loss, or impose a meaning the family may not share.

quiz.q: A nonverbal patient with dementia grimaces and pulls away each time her hip is moved. How should a tech document and report this?
choices: "Pain 7 out of 10 in the right hip"
"Denies pain"
"Grimaces and withdraws the right leg with movement; heart rate rises from 78 to 102"
"Appears comfortable"
quiz.why: Objective behavioral and physiologic findings are the valid report for a patient who cannot self-rate. Assigning a number fabricates data, and 'denies pain' or 'appears comfortable' both misrepresent a patient who is showing pain behavior.

quiz.q: Postmortem care in a non-ME case should be completed within what window, and why?
choices: Within 30 minutes, to free the room
Within 2 to 4 hours, before rigor mortis sets in
Within 12 hours, before the body is released
There is no time constraint
quiz.why: Rigor mortis begins around 2 to 4 hours. Once it sets, the eyes and mouth cannot be closed and limbs cannot be straightened, which affects the family's viewing. Room turnover and release timing are administrative, not physiologic.

scenarios.title: Bed 14: an 84-year-old boarding since this morning
scenarios.intro:
It is 1900. Mrs. Okafor, 84, came in at 0900 with a urinary tract infection and confusion. She was admitted at 1300 but there are no inpatient beds, so she has been on an ED stretcher for ten hours. She has a history of dementia, walks at home with a walker, and takes a diuretic. Her daughter just left for the night.

The night nurse asks you to "get her settled." You pull back the blanket and find her gown and the sheet beneath her are wet with urine. She is picking at the sheet and trying to swing a leg over the rail.

steps.prompt: She is agitated, soaked, and half over the rail. The bed is at hip height from the last blood draw and two rails are down. What do you do first?

choices.text: Put the bed in the lowest position, raise the two rails nearest her, and stay at the bedside while you call for a second person
choices.feedback: Correct. A patient mid-climb from a high bed is the immediate danger. Lower and lock first, get a rail between her and the floor, and do not leave her to go find help — call from the room.

choices.text: Step out to the supply room to get clean linen and a brief before anything else
choices.feedback: Harmful. She is already over the rail on a high bed. Leaving the room is how this becomes a fall from hip height with a head strike. Linen can wait sixty seconds.

choices.text: Raise all four side rails so she cannot get out, then go get supplies
choices.feedback: Harmful. Four rails is a physical restraint requiring an order, and a determined patient simply goes over the foot of the bed from a greater height. It also does not address the high bed.

choices.text: Hold her shoulders down and tell her firmly to stay in bed
choices.feedback: Not acceptable. Physically holding her down is a restraint without an order, and shouting at a delirious 84-year-old escalates the agitation. Lower the bed instead.

steps.prompt: The bed is low and locked and a second tech is with you. Mrs. Okafor keeps saying "I need to go, I need to go." You are about to clean her up. How do you start?

choices.text: Say her name, tell her you are going to help her get clean and dry and then get her to the bathroom, and ask if that is okay
choices.feedback: Right. Naming her, naming the plan and asking permission is what converts an assault into care — and it also answers her actual complaint, which is that she needs to urinate.

choices.text: Pull the gown off and begin washing without speaking, since she has dementia and will not remember
choices.feedback: Wrong on both counts. Dementia does not remove the right to be told what is happening, and unexplained touch is the single most reliable way to make a delirious patient combative.

choices.text: Tell her she already has a brief on and does not need the bathroom
choices.feedback: This is how learned incontinence starts, and it ignores that her stated need is the reason she is trying to climb out. Toileting her is the intervention.

choices.text: Explain what you are doing as you go, but start immediately because the room is needed
choices.feedback: Explaining is good. Skipping the request for permission and rushing a confused patient usually costs you more time than it saves when she resists.

steps.prompt: You get her clean. Washing her, you notice a red area over her sacrum. You press it for three seconds and it stays red. Both heels are also red.

choices.text: Report it to the nurse now as non-blanchable erythema, document it, offload the heels with a pillow under the calves, and reposition her off her back
choices.feedback: Exactly right. Non-blanchable means stage 1 — capillaries already damaged. Reporting and charting it in the ED documents when it appeared, and floating the heels and turning her stop it progressing.

choices.text: Massage the sacrum and both heels to bring circulation back
choices.feedback: Harmful. Massaging a damaged bony prominence shears the remaining capillaries and makes the injury worse. This is a specifically contraindicated action.

choices.text: Put a donut cushion under her sacrum and a rolled towel under each heel
choices.feedback: Both are wrong tools. A donut creates a ring of ischemia around the area, and a roll under the heels relocates pressure rather than removing it. The pillow goes under the calves.

choices.text: Note it and mention it at shift change so the oncoming tech can watch it
choices.feedback: Too slow. A stage 1 injury reported hours later loses the documentation that it was present during this stay, and she stays on her back in the meantime.

steps.prompt: She is clean, dry, turned onto a 30-degree tilt with heels floated, and calmer. She says she still needs to urinate and asks to walk to the bathroom. She uses a walker at home. Her diuretic was given at 1600.

choices.text: Check the activity order, sit her on the edge of the bed for 1 to 2 minutes, ask about dizziness, put non-skid socks on her, apply a gait belt, and walk her with two people and her walker
choices.feedback: This is the whole sequence. The diuretic plus ten hours flat makes her orthostatic until proven otherwise, and the dangle is what catches it before she is standing.

choices.text: Bring her a bedpan instead, since she is confused and it is faster
choices.feedback: Acceptable if she truly cannot walk, but she ambulates at home and immobility is part of what is hurting her. Defaulting to the pan without trying is how ED patients lose function.

choices.text: Help her straight up out of bed and walk her to the bathroom yourself
choices.feedback: Harmful. No dangle, no dizziness check, no footwear, one person. She is on a diuretic and has been recumbent for ten hours — this is the setup for a syncopal fall in the hallway.

choices.text: Tell her to wait until the nurse can assess her
choices.feedback: Delaying toileting is the leading trigger for an unassisted attempt and a fall. Ambulating a patient is within your role once you have checked the activity order.

steps.prompt: She dangles for 90 seconds and says the room is "going gray." Her repeat standing blood pressure is 102/58 from a lying 134/76.

choices.text: Lie her back down, tell the nurse she is symptomatically orthostatic with a 32 mmHg systolic drop, and offer a bedside commode or bedpan instead
choices.feedback: Correct on every count. Symptoms plus a drop well past 20 mmHg systolic is orthostatic hypotension. You report the number, not just 'she felt dizzy', and you still solve her toileting need.

choices.text: Have her keep sitting for another five minutes, then try standing again
choices.feedback: Sitting her back is reasonable, but a symptomatic 32 mmHg drop after a diuretic is a finding the nurse needs now, not after a second attempt.

choices.text: Support her under both arms and walk her quickly to the bathroom before she gets worse
choices.feedback: Harmful twice over. You are walking a patient who is actively presyncopal, and lifting under the arms dislocates shoulders. This is the fall.

choices.text: Put her back to bed and chart 'patient refused ambulation'
choices.feedback: Factually wrong and it hides a real finding. She did not refuse — she became symptomatic. Charting it as refusal buries the orthostatic drop the team needs to see.

scenarios.debrief:
The pattern: **a boarding elderly patient is an inpatient in a room designed for twenty minutes of care.** Everything that went wrong for Mrs. Okafor came from time on a hard surface with nobody doing basic care — unmet toileting drove the agitation and the climb attempt, ten hours of pressure produced the stage 1 sacrum and heels, and ten hours flat plus a diuretic produced the orthostatic drop.

The order of operations is the lesson. Make it safe first (bed low, locked, rail, second person), then explain and get permission, then care and assess while you wash, then mobilize with a dangle and a real assessment before the feet take weight. Report numbers, not impressions: non-blanchable erythema, 32 mmHg systolic drop, output measured in milliliters. And never chart a symptom as a refusal.

scenarios.title: Hall bed 3: the swallow, the tray, and the family
scenarios.intro:
Mr. Duarte, 76, arrived at 1400 with right-sided weakness and slurred speech. Time last known well was 1315. He got a CT, the stroke team saw him, and he is now in hall bed 3 waiting for an inpatient bed. He is awake and follows commands. His speech is thick but understandable.

It is 1830 and dietary just delivered dinner trays down the hall. Mr. Duarte's son is at the bedside and has a cup of coffee and a straw.

steps.prompt: You walk up and the son is holding the straw to his father's lips. "He's been asking for a drink for two hours." There is no swallow screen documented and the chart says NPO.

choices.text: Ask him to stop, explain that a swallow check has to be passed first because a stroke can affect swallowing, and get the nurse
choices.feedback: Correct, and the explanation matters — the son is not being difficult, he is trying to help his father. Telling him why turns him into an ally for the rest of the stay.

choices.text: Let him finish the sip since it is only coffee, then mention it later
choices.feedback: Harmful. Thin liquid through a straw delivers a fast bolus to the throat of a patient whose swallow has not been tested. This is the highest-risk combination there is.

choices.text: Take the cup out of his hand without explanation and walk away with it
choices.feedback: The action is right and the manner is wrong. An unexplained confiscation makes the family hide the next attempt rather than ask you about it.

choices.text: Offer to bring ice chips instead, which are gentler
choices.feedback: Wrong. An ice chip is water. NPO includes ice, and substituting it yourself is making a diet decision that is not yours to make.

steps.prompt: The nurse performs a bedside swallow screen. He passes with thin liquids and a regular diet is ordered. His mouth is dry and coated after five hours NPO. He wants to eat now, and the tray is here.

choices.text: Do oral care first, then sit him fully upright at 90 degrees, set up the tray within reach of his working left hand, and stay to supervise
choices.feedback: Right. Oral care before eating reduces the bacterial load that turns any aspiration into pneumonia, and upright plus a tray on the functional side is the setup.

choices.text: Hand him the tray and raise the head of the bed to 30 degrees so he can rest while he eats
choices.feedback: Thirty degrees is a reclining position and lets food travel by gravity toward an airway that may still be slow. Fully upright is the requirement, not a comfort preference.

choices.text: Sit him up and give him the tray, skipping oral care since he is hungry and it has been five hours
choices.feedback: The position is right. Skipping oral care after five hours NPO leaves a mouth full of bacteria, which is what makes an aspiration event turn into pneumonia.

choices.text: Place the tray on his right side so he practices using his weak arm
choices.feedback: Not now. Putting the tray out of reach of his functional hand means he leans, reaches, or gives up eating. Therapy for the weak side is a rehabilitation decision, not a dinner tray decision.

steps.prompt: He is upright, mouth cleaned, eating. Three bites in, he coughs twice. You ask him to say his name. His voice sounds wet and bubbly. The portable monitor shows his saturation sliding.

choices.text: Stop the meal, keep him fully upright, check that suction is set up at the bedside, and get the nurse immediately
choices.feedback: Exactly right. Coughing plus a wet voice plus desaturation is aspiration until proven otherwise. Upright, suction ready, nurse now — in that order.

choices.text: Give him a sip of water to clear his throat
choices.feedback: Harmful. You are adding thin liquid to an airway that just proved it cannot protect itself. This is the most common instinctive wrong move at the bedside.

choices.text: Lay him flat and turn his head to the side
choices.feedback: Harmful here. Lying him flat removes the only protection gravity is giving. The lateral position is for an unresponsive patient who is actively vomiting, not for an awake patient who is aspirating food.

choices.text: Pause the meal, watch him for a minute, and resume if the cough settles
choices.feedback: Pausing is right and waiting is wrong. He passed a screen and is still showing signs, which is information the nurse and the stroke team need before another bite goes in.

steps.prompt: The nurse comes, he clears with suction, and his saturation returns to 96%. He is made NPO again pending a formal speech-language pathology evaluation. His son is upset: "You people said he could eat."

choices.text: Acknowledge that it is frustrating, explain plainly that a screen can be passed and swallowing can still fail, say the speech therapist will do a full evaluation, and offer him a chair and water for himself
choices.feedback: This is service recovery done right. You validate the feeling, give a truthful explanation with no jargon and no blame, name the next step, and attend to the family member as a person.

choices.text: Explain that his father should never have had the coffee earlier and that may be why
choices.feedback: Blaming the family is both unkind and probably untrue — the aspiration happened with food, after a passed screen. It also guarantees he stops telling you things.

choices.text: Tell him you only follow orders and the nurse made the decision
choices.feedback: Deflecting onto a colleague damages the team in front of the family and answers none of his actual question. You can explain the reasoning without owning the decision.

choices.text: Apologize and get the nurse to explain it
choices.feedback: Not wrong, and the nurse should follow up. But you were in the room, you saw it, and you can explain what happened in plain words right now rather than leaving him with nothing.

steps.prompt: He is stable, NPO, and will board overnight. Before you leave the hall bed at shift change, what do you do and what do you hand off?

choices.text: Oral care with a moist swab and no free water, bed low and locked, call bell in his left hand, reposition him, and hand off the aspiration event with the SpO2 numbers, the NPO status and the pending SLP evaluation
choices.feedback: Complete. The parched NPO patient still gets mouth care with no free water, the fall and pressure basics still apply, and the handoff carries the event, the numbers and the pending order rather than 'he had a rough evening'.

choices.text: Give him a cup of water and a straw at the bedside so he can wet his mouth overnight
choices.feedback: Harmful. He is NPO after an aspiration event. Leaving thin liquid and a straw within reach of a patient with a stroke is the exact setup you just spent an hour undoing.

choices.text: Chart 'patient tolerated diet poorly' and tell the night tech he is NPO
choices.feedback: Too vague. 'Tolerated poorly' does not convey a witnessed aspiration with desaturation to 91%, and the night shift needs the numbers and the pending SLP consult to know what they are watching for.

choices.text: Reposition him, lower the bed and hand off verbally, but skip oral care since he is NPO and nothing is going in his mouth
choices.feedback: Backwards. NPO patients need oral care more, not less — five hours of dry mouth grows exactly the bacteria that turn a small aspiration into pneumonia.

scenarios.debrief:
Two patterns here. The first is **NPO is a safety order, not a formality** — it includes ice, it includes what a well-meaning family brings in, and a tech who explains why gets cooperation instead of a hidden straw. The second is that **a passed screen is a snapshot, not a guarantee.** Swallowing fatigues; a stroke patient who cleared thin liquids at 1830 can aspirate a solid bolus three bites later.

The bedside signs are the same every time: cough or throat-clearing, a wet or gurgly voice when you ask them to speak, drooling or pocketing, and a saturation that slides during the meal. The response is the same every time: stop, stay upright, suction available, call. Never water, never flat.

And two things that look optional and are not — oral care on the NPO patient, because pooled oral bacteria are what make aspiration lethal, and a handoff with actual numbers in it.
